content: To implement the WHO postnatal care model effectively, several system-level and user-level considerations must be addressed: 1. System-Level Considerations: National and subnational working groups should be established to adapt and implement the WHO postnatal care recommendations. This includes revising or developing national and subnational guidelines and protocols based on the WHO model. Long-term planning is essential to address shortages of skilled health personnel and trained community health workers. This also involves improving health facility infrastructure, referral pathways, and ensuring the sustainability of high-quality postnatal care services. Pre-service training institutions and professional bodies should be involved to update postnatal care training curricula promptly and efficiently. In-service training and supervisory models must be developed to meet the professional requirements of health workers. These models should address content, duration, and selection criteria for training while also mitigating staff turnover, especially in low-resource settings. Standardized tools for supervision should be created to enable supervisors to support health workers in delivering integrated and comprehensive postnatal care services. A task-sharing strategy may be necessary to optimize the use of human resources. Implementation tools or job aids for health facilities and community-level care should be developed or updated to align with the postnatal care model. Strategies to improve supply chain management should be devised, including protocols for obtaining and maintaining stock levels, monitoring supply data, and enhancing coordination for medicines and healthcare supplies. National guidelines and facility-based protocols should be revised or developed in line with WHO postnatal care recommendations. Successful implementation strategies should be documented and shared as best practices for other implementers. 2. User-Level Considerations: Community sensitization activities should be conducted to disseminate information about the importance of postnatal care, including women’s and babies’ rights to receive such care. This should include details about the timing, content of recommended contacts, and any associated user fees. Postnatal care services and client flow may need to be reorganized to reduce waiting times. 3. Dissemination of Guidelines: The guideline will be disseminated through WHO regional and country offices, ministries of health, professional organizations, collaborating centers, UN agencies, NGOs, and professional associations. It will also be available on the WHO website and as a printed publication. Online versions will be accessible via relevant WHO department websites. Technical meetings will be held between WHO and stakeholders to share recommendations and derivative products. Updated recommendations will also be shared during scientific conferences and meetings attended by WHO maternal and perinatal staff. Evidence briefs highlighting recommendations and contextual implementation issues will be developed for policymakers, program managers, and health workers in collaboration with organizations such as FIGO, ICM, IPA, UNFPA, UNICEF, and USAID. The executive summary and recommendations will be translated into six UN languages for broader dissemination. 4. Monitoring and Evaluation: The implementation and impact of the recommendations will be monitored at health service, subnational, and national levels using clearly defined criteria and indicators aligned with locally agreed targets. Data on the adoption of recommendations will be collected and evaluated in the short to medium term through the WHO SRMNCAH Policy Survey. A full monitoring framework will be developed once the guidelines are finalized. In the interim, suggested indicators include the length of stay in health facilities after childbirth, early routine postnatal care for newborns, and the percentage of children receiving the hepatitis B birth dose vaccine within 24 hours of birth. 5. Updating the Guidelines: A systematic and continuous process will be employed to identify and address evidence gaps following guideline implementation. An Executive Guideline Steering Group (GSG) for maternal and newborn health recommendations will convene biannually to review and prioritize new and existing questions for recommendation development and updating. Recommendations will be regularly reviewed and updated as new evidence emerges. If no new evidence is identified, recommendations will be revalidated. Any concerns about the validity of recommendations will be promptly communicated, and updates will be planned as needed.
